children: Iron ore futures rose on Thursday as signs of easing coking coal supply constraints and a pickup in blast furnace activity pointed to improving steel mill demand, while higher maritime freight rates and stronger steel exports added further support.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
closed daytime trade 1.32% higher at 726.50 yuan ($108.15) a metric ton.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was 2.17% higher at $99.40 a ton.

A recent correction in Dalian coking coal futures signals that domestic supply constraints, driven by increased mine safety scrutiny and inspections, may be easing, said Atilla Widnell, managing director at Navigate Commodities.
Daily thermal satellite monitoring of 288 blast furnaces and 365 coke ovens across China shows both clusters have been steadily ramping up capacity utilisation since August 25, Widnell said.
Maritime freight rates remained elevated, providing cost support, analysts from Chinese broker GF Futures said in a note.
Freight rates on major routes to China rose on Wednesday, Mysteel data showed. Higher freight rates tend to support seaborne iron ore prices.

China's total steel exports rose 7.8% week-on-week to 2.55 million tons in the week to August 31, marking the third straight weekly increase and the highest level in nearly eight weeks, Mysteel data showed. On a yearly basis, exports were up 23.9%.
